People assume that because I defend the scheme in public I think it is perfect. I have spent six years listing its faults in private, which is a strange way to live.
Then start with the strongest objection. Not the one you find easiest to answer.
Fair. The strongest is that it is regressive at the bottom of the scale. Granted. That is real, it is measurable, and my side tends to change the subject when it comes up.
That the rebate offsets most of it, though not all, and that the alternative on the table was worse in the same direction. Both of those are defensible. Neither of them makes the objection go away.
Admittedly that is more honest than most of what I read about it. Although I notice you have not said whether you would vote for it.
I would, and with reservations I would say out loud. For all its faults it did the thing it was built to do. That said, if you asked me to design it again, I would not design that.
Which is a sentence I wish I heard more often from people who are paid to be certain.

A brief note on how this was actually introduced, because the sequence matters. It was rolled out in four regions first, deliberately chosen to be different from one another, and it ran there for eighteen months before anybody committed to going further. It is now being phased in nationally over six years, which is a long time, and I would say frankly that six years is a political number rather than an economic one. Two things happened that were not in the plan. An unintended consequence appeared in the rental market inside the first year, and it took another year to measure properly. And for the very largest firms the first stage produced a windfall, most of which the treasury clawed back through the tax code, though not all of it, and not quickly.

Let me start with what I accept, because I think my colleagues on this side skip it too quickly. Waiting times fell. That is real, it is measured, and it is not a rounding error. Granted also that the scheme was introduced carefully, in four regions, and that whoever designed the sequence knew what they were doing. And I accept that the alternative under discussion at the time was in some respects worse. That said, my objection stands, and it is this. It is a blunt instrument. A targeted scheme would have achieved most of the same result for considerably less money, and the reason we did not build one is that targeting is administratively hard and politically thankless. I am not arguing that anybody acted in bad faith. I am arguing that we chose the easy design and then congratulated ourselves on the outcome.

She says she would vote for it with reservations, and would not design it that way again.
